study.title: Test Lab
study.question: How do I know if my product really works?
study.passage:
Testing plan (written for this lesson), using the bookmark challenge:
Criterion 1: Size is 5 cm by 20 cm (± 2 mm). Test: measure with a ruler.
Criterion 2: Survives 20 uses. Test: put the bookmark in a paperback and close and open the book 20 times; check for tears or bends.
Criterion 3: Slogan readable from 1 m. Test: three classmates read it from 1 m; record how many read it correctly.
Criterion 4: Costs under 10 dirhams for 30. Test: add up the cost of materials used.
Criterion 5: No sharp edges. Test: run a finger carefully along each edge.
Rules for fair testing: test every bookmark the same way; record results right away; don't skip a test because you think it will pass.
Results table: For each criterion, record the result and mark Pass or Fail.

body.objective: Students will be able to give and use peer feedback.
body.iCan: I can give and use peer feedback.
successCriteria: I can give specific, kind and helpful feedback
I can receive feedback without getting defensive
I can decide which feedback to use
body.hook: Pixar shows unfinished films to the whole studio and invites brutally honest notes. Their directors say the first version of every film "sucks," and feedback is how it gets better. Good feedback is a gift, if you know how to give it and use it.

vocabulary.definition: Comments that help someone improve their work.
A classmate or someone at the same level.
Clear and detailed, pointing to exactly what works or needs work.
Aimed at helping improve, not at criticizing the person.
A feedback method: one thing that works (glow) and one thing to improve (grow).

study.title: Gallery Walk Feedback
study.question: How can feedback from others improve my product?
study.passage:
Feedback protocol (written for this lesson):
1. Set up: Each team places its product with its criteria checklist.
2. Gallery walk (15 minutes): Visit three other products. For each, write one "glow" and one "grow" on sticky notes. Each comment must point to a criterion.
Strong examples: "Glow: the slogan is easy to read from across the room." "Grow: the corners bent after a few uses; try rounding them or using thicker card."
Weak examples: "Nice!" "It's bad." "I don't like the colour."
3. Read your feedback (5 minutes): Don't argue or explain. Sort the notes into three piles: "Use it," "Maybe," "Not this time."
4. Respond (10 minutes): Choose the two most useful notes and write how you will act on them.

body.objective: Students will be able to plan an improvement.
successCriteria: I can use test results and feedback to find what to improve
I can choose the improvement that matters most

body.hook: The first iPhone had no copy-and-paste and no app store. Each new version fixed what users complained about. Real products are never finished on the first try; they are improved one planned change at a time.

vocabulary.definition: A change that makes a product better meet its criteria.

To give reasons and evidence for a decision.

study.title: Version 2.0
study.question: How do I decide what to improve first?
study.passage:
Improvement planner (written for this lesson):
Step 1, Gather evidence: List every failed criterion from your tests and every "use it" feedback note.
Step 2, Rate each problem: Impact (how much fixing it helps meet the brief, 1–3) and Effort (how much time or material it takes, 1–3).
Step 3, Choose: Fix high-impact, low-effort problems first. Consider trade-offs: thicker card fixes bending but may raise the cost.
Step 4, Plan: Write exactly what you will change, the materials and time needed, and how you will test it again.
Sample problem list (bookmark challenge): corners bend after 5 uses (impact 3, effort 1); slogan smudges (impact 2, effort 2); colours not school colours (impact 1, effort 1); cost 12 dirhams for 30, over budget (impact 3, effort 2).
